Doing that gives us a way to show local institutions where waste disposal services are lacking and talk about what needs to change.

items.title: Big Tech, AI, and the quiet expansion of digital surveillance in Nigeria

s: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?
Every search, social media interaction, and conversation with an artificial intelligence (AI) tool can leave behind information about its user.
Individually, these digital traces may appear insignificant.
Collectively, however, they can reveal interests, habits, preferences and patterns of behavior that have considerable commercial and political value.
As AI becomes increasingly embedded in everyday life, technology companies are finding new ways to use data to develop their products, personalize services and generate revenue.
While these developments offer considerable benefits, they also raise a difficult question: How much control do people retain over their personal information in a world increasingly shaped by AI?
The issue extends beyond privacy policies and user agreements.

It concerns the growing power of technology companies to collect information, draw conclusions about individuals, and influence the digital environments in which people communicate, work, and access information.

In September 2024, the United States Federal Trade Commission (FTC) published findings from an investigation into nine major social media and video-streaming companies, including Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and Amazon-owned Twitch.
The FTC reported that these companies collected extensive information about users and, in some cases, non-users.
The information included personal details, interests, online activities, and data obtained from other sources.
The investigation also raised concerns about lengthy data retention, inadequate privacy protections, and the use of personal information in automated systems, including AI.

The report highlighted a fundamental imbalance: Companies can accumulate substantial information about individuals, while those individuals may have limited understanding of how their data is used or how to prevent certain uses.
AI adds another dimension to this problem.
Data can help train models, improve recommendations, and power automated decisions.
However, the greater the volume and variety of information companies can access, the more important it becomes to establish clear limits on its collection and use.
The concern is not that every company collecting data is necessarily acting maliciously.
Rather, it is that systems designed to maximize commercial value from information can create incentives to collect more data than people reasonably expect or understand.
For millions of people, AI offers opportunities that were previously difficult to access.
Students can use AI tools to support learning, small businesses can improve their operations, and journalists can explore new approaches to research and production.
In countries such as Nigeria, where access to resources and professional services can be uneven, these tools could help narrow certain gaps.
AI systems that support local languages and reflect diverse cultural experiences could also make digital services more accessible.
Yet inclusion should mean more than allowing people to use a technology.
It should also mean ensuring that they understand the conditions under which they use it and retain meaningful rights over their information.
Many digital services are governed by lengthy terms and privacy policies that users may accept without fully understanding the implications.
Some AI products also raise questions about whether information submitted through prompts, uploaded documents, or other interactions may be retained or used to improve models.
The precise practices differ between companies and products.
Nevertheless, users need clear explanations of what information is collected, why it is needed, how long it is retained, and whether it may be used for purposes beyond the immediate service.
Without these safeguards, the benefits of AI inclusion risk coming with an invisible cost: reduced control over personal information.
The connection between big tech and authoritarianism requires careful examination.
Authoritarianism is not simply the collection of data by private companies.
It involves the concentration and exercise of power in ways that undermine accountability, rights, and freedoms.
However, extensive corporate data collection can create conditions that make surveillance easier.
Detailed personal information can support profiling, targeted persuasion and the prediction of individual behavior.
Depending on the circumstances, businesses, governments, or other actors may exploit these capabilities.

items.title: Global Voices condemns the attacks on Albanian fact-checking service Faktoje

s: Faktoje is a respected member of the international fact-checking community

Since October 27, at least 20 online media outlets and social media accounts in Albania have been waging a coordinated attack against the staff of fact-checking media service Faktoje Center, based in Tirana.
A partner of Global Voices, Faktoje has been promoting accountability based on the right to information and transparency since 2018.

Faktoje and its team members, in particular its director, Klodiana Kapo, are facing a series of coordinated attacks from media outlets that have been circulating and reproducing articles that question Faktoje’s funding, financial management and independence, using its publicly available financial statements to cast doubt on the organisation’s credibility.
Faktoje is a certified signatory of the Code of Principles of the International Fact-Finding Network and the Code of Standards of the European Fact-Checking Standards Network.
Both require high levels of public transparency in disclosing sources of funding and methodologies of work.

This coordinated campaign aims to undermine the impact of Faktoje’s important work by maliciously using financial information that the organization voluntarily publishes, but stripping it of context and mischaracterizing its influence.

Faktoje considers these attacks to be directly connected to its fact-checking activities under its partnership with Meta, in the context of its recent fact-checking work covering the ongoing protests and debunking misleading narratives targeting protesters.

Since its inception eight years ago, Faktoje has stood at the forefront of the fight for freedom of expression, independent journalism, and information integrity in Albania and the wider Balkans region, including participation in the regional Western Balkans Anti-Disinformation Hub, the Anti-Disinformation Network for the Balkans and the continent-wide European Digital Media Observatory – EDMO Network.
Faktoje is a respected member of the international fact-checking community.

Albanian authorities and European institutions need to speak up publicly for independent fact-checkers and journalists, and to ensure their safety, while media outlets reporting on civil society funding need to do so accurately and in context.
Global Voices joins the European Fact-Checking Standards Network and the International Fact-Checking Network in vehemently condemning those attacks on our partner.
We stand in solidarity with our colleagues.

items.title: Venezuela welcomes opposition leader María Corina Machado home

s: María Corina Machado arriving in Caracas after months of hiding and exile.
Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026.
Used with permission.

Thousands of people took to the Valle-Coche highway in Caracas to welcome the opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate María Corina Machado, who returned to Venezuela after 16 months in hiding and ten months in exile.
The massive gathering was one of celebration, but her compatriots were also filled with doubts about what comes next.

After more than a year in the shadows, forced into hiding following her kidnapping — allegedly by government paramilitaries — at her last public protest in 2025, Machado quietly slipped out of the country.

She emerged on the global stage later that year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize honoring her social organization campaign during Venezuela’s 2024 presidential elections, which were ultimately stolen by Nicolás Maduro.

Since the former Venezuelan president’s capture on January 3, 2026, Machado has tried — and failed — to enter the country on at least seven occasions, claiming that the administration established by U.S.
President Donald Trump didn’t allow her in.

On the morning of October 25, however, Machado was spotted in the city of Barquisimeto, where she visited the Santa Rosa church, and at about 10:25 that evening, her caravan passed through Santa Mónica, along the main route that leads to Venezuela’s captital:
Drivers excitedly honked their horns; in a crowd of about 3,000, people shouted slogans.
Starting from the state of Lara, Machado’s caravan crossed Yaracuy, Carabobo, and Aragua as it inched toward Caracas — a journey of more than 300 kilometres that took her nearly 11 hours to complete.

On the heels of the January 3 United States military operation that captured Nicolás Maduro, whose 2024 re-election was questioned both inside and outside of Venezuela, then vice president Delcy Rodríguez took over as interim president.
Since August, her interim government has been negotiating with Dinorah Figuera, president of the National Assembly who was elected in 2015, in a Washington-driven dialogue process.
Despite having promoted participation in the 2024 presidential elections, Machado’s party, Vente Venezuela, has had no representation in those negotiations.
The crowd waited for hours for Maria Corina Machado's arrival to the capital city.
Photo by Óscar Calles, 2026.
Used with permission.
Yet, U.S.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio attributed Machado’s safe return to those talks, which he claimed had already allowed for the release of hundreds of political prisoners and the return of hundreds of exiled opposition figures.
Rubio called on all political actors to back them because they represent “the best opportunity Venezuela has had in thirty years.”

Faced with political demobilization, Venezuelans are used to seeing protests where the majority of participants are activists, leaders, and members of civil society organizations — people who are well-informed because it is their job to be — but Machado’s gathering was different.
There were people without party shirts or hats; just a combination of families, friends, and civilians who seemed motivated by her return and hopeful for their country.
People began to assemble on the highway around 3:00 p.m. local time.
After hours of waiting, the gathering turned into a party — the type of celebration that many did not dare to have after January 3.
Machado barely spoke; she did not have a megaphone and was in the tray of a pickup truck with a security detail around her.
She gave no statements to the media during the caravan; instead, she listened to and greeted the crowd, hugging people, touching their hands, and letting herself be seen.
On this occasion, people did not go to hear proposals, but simply to see her.
October’s Spotlight contributors illuminated a range of political, economic, and geographic contexts

Fifteen years ago I wrote an article about “networked authoritarianism,” describing China as “exhibit A” for how an authoritarian state adapts to the internet and then adapts digital technologies to increase its own power.
I sought to counter prevailing narratives of the time that the internet and tech companies were intrinsically a liberating, democratizing force.
While such narratives were eventually discredited, we must not give up on our ability to use technology to defend and exercise our rights.
Nor can we simply demand that governments and companies solve the problems they jointly continue to create.
October’s spotlight on Big Tech and Authoritarianism explored a range of relationships between tech companies and political actors across the global majority.
Power is wielded through digital technologies in many ways.
There are no quick fixes or easy solutions to stop abuses.

But we are not helpless: our Global Voices community has a role to play in strengthening solidarity and cooperation among people fighting to defend their rights, hold abusers accountable, and claim agency over our information environments.
Spotlight contributors illuminated a range of political, economic, and geographic contexts: from Brazil to Hong Kong, Kenya, Myanmar, Palestine, Venezuela, Xinjiang and beyond.

They’ve told stories of how different types of governments (or sometimes political insurgents) leverage geopolitical alliances, relationships with tech companies, regulatory power, or other advantages in order to expand political or military dominance, manipulate public opinion, or exercise direct control over citizens.
Meanwhile, companies use their own technologies, resources, and government relationships to expand market access and profit.
Tech power is often wielded in ways that make it harder for ordinary people to fight back against abuses.
In some cases it is difficult, if not impossible, to prove who has committed what abuse and whether it was intentional — even while harm to individuals or communities has clearly occurred.
In other cases, companies discover abuse of their systems to threaten, silence, surveil, or mislead users only after the damage has been done.
In Brazil, one expert warns of “governance washing.
An NGO leader working in West Asia and North Africa warns of the rise of a cottage industry of organizations focused on tech accountability without measurably preventing harms.
In North America and Europe, government regulation of Big Tech is often touted as a silver bullet for protecting citizens from harm.

But stories from Bangladesh, Kenya and the DRC illustrate different ways that without rigorous safeguards, regulation and enforcement in the name of holding Big Tech accountable can be abused by governments to threaten, track, or discredit critics and political rivals.
Our contributors pointed to conditions that must be met if we are to prevent government abuse of regulations.
Laws and regulations need to be evaluated for their compatibility with human rights standards, and reformed or rejected if they fall short.

Citizens — through the free press, watchdog NGOs, whistleblower protections and grievance mechanisms — need to be able to monitor and document harms and abuses with clear process for redress and remedy.
Sadly, most democracies fail to hold governments — let alone companies — accountable for protecting human rights.
Then there is the even harder problem of what multinational companies should do after a coup or military takeover, leaving users’ data exposed with deadly consequences.
Such cases underscore the vital importance of encryption, data security training for civil society, and corporate data minimization practices.
A number of stories describe how global powers leverage their national tech companies to advance strategic and economic interests well beyond their own borders.
The companies in turn benefit from such relationships to expand their own global market access, serving as opaque information intermediaries and channels of digital infrastructure.

items.title: The scandals and suspects surrounding Flávio Bolsonaro, according to the Brazilian press

s: After being defeated in the elections, the senator fled to the US with his family
Art by Global Voices with Canva Pro.
Photo by the Brazilian Senate. Fair use.

Forty-eight hours after losing the runoff in Brazil to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Flávio Bolsonaro, former president Jair Bolsonaro ’s eldest son, a senator representing Rio de Janeiro, fled to the United States.

From there, where his brother Eduardo, a former congressman, has lived since February 2025, he continues to challenge the results of the election he lost by 4.4 million votes, as attested by the Electoral Court (TSE), the Organization of American States (OAS), and other right-led governments in the region.
Upon landing in Miami, Flávio published a letter proclaiming himself “the true president of Brazil” and “president-elect of Brazil.
After 22 minutes — and a demand from the US Department of State — he retracted to “the leader of Brazil.”
US President Donald Trump had said that Brazil’s elections “ looked rigged,” but he wouldn't “ get involved.
The New York Times reported, however, that Flávio was helped by Trump's aides.
“The jet [he traveled on] had been arranged by a White House official,” affirmed the newspaper.

Flávio’s narrative is that he is being persecuted by the Brazilian justice system and Lula’s government as an opposition leader, since the Supreme Court ordered the seizure of his passports — he also has Italian citizenship — right after his defeat was announced.

Justice Alexandre de Moraes, considered a foe of the Bolsonaro family and himself under suspicion for having links to the same disgraced banker connected to Flávio, issued the order in response to a Federal Police request that considered Flávio a flight risk.
In Brazil, a president cannot be investigated for alleged crimes committed before their term, meaning that once elected, all pending investigations involving Flávio would have been suspended.
This is also the first time in 24 years that Flávio will not have a seat to ensure his parliamentary immunity.

According to the Brazilian Federal Police, three elements indicated a flight risk in Flávio’s case: an interview his brother Eduardo gave to a podcast in the US defending the idea of him leaving the country, on October 23, his considerable economic power, and well-established structures abroad that could support him in a long stay.

The day after the election, after visiting his father, who is under house arrest convicted for a coup attempt, Flávio recorded a video complaining about the measure, claiming “he never thought about leaving the country” and promising to stay and answer to investigations.
Overnight, apparently, he had a change of heart in time for a new plan.
Investigations and corruption suspicions have long surrounded his name.

In 2020, Sergio Moro, the judge who convicted Lula, resigned as Bolsonaro’s justice minister, accusing the president of trying to intervene with the Federal Police to protect Flávio in an embezzlement and money-laundering inquiry.
In a cabinet meeting, then-president Bolsonaro shouted at his ministers: “I won’t wait until they fuck my entire family,” saying he would fire whoever got in their way.
During this election campaign, skeletons in Flávio's closet were further exposed in stories published by the Brazilian press.
Global Voices gathered the main ones here.
Flávio is currently under three investigations at the Supreme Court.
This is the case that led Jair Bolsonaro to allegedly interfere in the Federal Police in 2020.
Flávio was indicted by Rio’s Public Prosecution Office for embezzlement, money laundering, and criminal organization.
The case was later adjourned.
Rachadinha (“split” in English) is a salary kickback scheme in which a politician hires someone for a certain position and then reclaims part of their salary.

items.title: Unmarried Chinese women are rewriting the marriage script

s: Chinese women are challenging marriage pressures and redefining what it means to be single.
The marriage market at People’s Park in Shanghai, 2013.
Photo by Jpbowen via Wikimedia Commons, licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0.
On weekends at Shanghai’s People’s Park, umbrellas covered with handwritten sheets of paper line the paths.
Parents stand beside them, exchanging information about their unmarried children: age, height, education, income, and whether they own an apartment.
It is one of China’s most famous marriage markets — a place where private hopes and social expectations meet in public since 2005.
For years, the word shengnü (剩女), literally translated as “leftover women,” hovered over many of the women whose profiles appeared there.
The translation sounds strange in English because the original Chinese carries a sharper meaning.
The character sheng (剩) does not simply mean “remaining.
It suggests something left behind, something unused.
In everyday contexts, it can describe leftover food — something that has passed its ideal moment and may eventually be discarded.

When the term became popular in China in the late 2000s, it was used to describe unmarried urban women, often highly educated professionals, who were considered “too old” for marriage after their late twenties.
The label was not just a description of marital status.
It turned a personal choice into a social judgment.
But today, if you search Chinese media, the phrase shengnü appears far less frequently than it once did.

Instead, a more neutral term, zhonggnü (中女), literally translated as “middle or in-and-between women,” is now more often used to describe unmarried women in their thirties in both mainstream media and social platforms.
While the word has faded, many of the expectations behind it remain.
The language around unmarried women has become more circumspect, though still pointed.

Instead of openly calling women “leftover,” conversations often appear in softer forms: concerns about women being “too picky,” warnings about missing the “best age” for marriage and childbirth, or questions about why a successful woman still has not found a partner.

Instead of using the neutral term zhonggnü, which still highlights women’s age, some women have created new terms and spaces on social media platforms, such as Xiaohongshu and Douban, to discuss these pressures on their own terms.
For example, they have reframed the marriage debate to cuīhūn (催婚) — the repeated pressure from family members to marry — and kǒnghūn (恐婚) — the fear or hesitation surrounding marriage itself.
These words reveal a shift.
The conversation is no longer only about why women are failing to meet expectations.
Increasingly, women are asking whether those expectations should be followed at all.
On Xiaohongshu, a user writing under the name “十元尼美” (Ten Yuan Nimei) described seven years of pressure to marry, beginning when she graduated from university.
By 30, she wrote, the pressure had eased — not because her family had accepted her choices, but because people arranging introductions considered her too old for the matchmaking market.
At 34, she said, her parents had almost stopped asking.
Her advice to other women began with creating physical distance.
Moving from her home province of Hunan to Beijing had largely confined her parents’ pressure to phone calls; later, she moved to Spain.
“Sometimes, freedom comes not from persuasion, but from distance,” she wrote.
Other posts question the pressure itself.
One shared by the account “渭北春天树” carried the title —“Pressuring someone to marry is, at its core, a form of expulsion.
(催婚的本质是一种驱逐) These conversations no longer see shengnü or unmarried women as a problem, but are turning the conversation on its head to scrutinize traditional conservative family values.

items.title: Tracing the recruitment trap behind Russia’s war

s: No justice for Bangladeshi workers who are recruited into Russia’s war
War-wounded Bangladeshis in Russia plead to return home.
Screenshot from a YouTube report by Ekhon TV. Fair use.
Maksudur Rahman was 31 when a labor recruiter arrived in his hometown in Lakshmipur district, southeastern Bangladesh, with a job offer: becoming a janitor in Russia.
Nearly every family in the district has someone working overseas, so the pitch landed.
According to an international investigation, he borrowed money and paid the broker BDT 1.2 million (about USD 9,800).
For a household like his, that is a fortune, but the promised wages made the debt look manageable.
He signed up and flew out.
What followed had nothing to do with brooms.
Within weeks, he was on the front lines of Russia’s war in Ukraine.
He and three other Bangladeshi workers were handed a paper written in Russian — a language they did not understand — and told to sign.
Then came an army camp, where recruits were trained in drone tactics, medical evacuation, and heavy weapons.
When Rahman protested, a Russian commander replied through a translation app that his own agent had sent him there.
Workers in his group were threatened with ten-year jail terms and beaten, he said.
His story is a case study in how this insidious war pipeline operates: a local agent, a borrowed fortune, a contract nobody could read, and a war that was never part of the bargain.
But to understand how a man from Lakshmipur ended up in that camp, it’s important to look at the realities in Russia and what is driving these recruitment traps.
Russia has a manpower problem, and the figures are hard to wave away.
Enlistment into contract service dropped about 20 percent in the first quarter of 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier, according to international reporting relayed by Ukrainian outlets.
This deficit persists even though Moscow is offering signing packages of up to USD 80,000 and debt write-offs of up to USD 140,000.
Meanwhile, BBC and Mediazona journalists estimate there have been at least 300,000 Russian deaths since the war began on February 24, 2022, based on local obituaries.
Other Western intelligence estimates put Russian deaths near 500,000, with monthly casualties of 30,000 to 35,000.
One estimate says the country needs another 1.5 million workers to stabilize its labor market, and officials themselves expect a shortfall of 3.1 million people by 2030.
Because stricter migration rules have also pushed out roughly a million temporary workers, the army and the factories now compete for the same shrinking labor pool.

While Russia has not dared to implement another full-scale military draft as it did in September 2022 — a move that was highly damaging to the regime and local support — officials are doing everything they can to buy recruits or force those who are vulnerable, elderly, or simply went to the draft station to register to go to the front lines.
Given these manpower challenges, Moscow has looked outward.
It has already used tens of thousands of prisoners and three waves of North Korean troops, yet that wasn’t enough.

A UK defense assessment, summarized by a Ukrainian outlet, says the supply of convict recruits is probably exhausted, and Russia is widening its search across the Global South to avoid another mobilization at home.
Ukrainian data counts nearly 29,000 foreigners who have signed contracts since 2022.
One report says the army wants at least 18,500 more in 2026, naming Bangladesh among its top targets.
Rights groups see a pattern behind these numbers.

The International Federation for Human Rights described an organized pipeline aimed at undocumented migrants, detainees, precarious workers, and foreign students across three continents, and Amnesty International accused Moscow last month of deceptive, coercive, and exploitative recruitment.

items.title: Egypt’s crackdown on independent media reaches Mada Masr as editor faces trial

s: Egypt convicted Mada Masr's Lina Attalah in a hearing marred by violations and ordered it closed
Lina Attalah.
Picture from Mada Masr website.
Used with permission.

The latest wave of suppression of the country’s last remaining critical voices began with the violent arrest of the entire newsroom of Matsada2sh, a fact-checking and open-source intelligence (OSINT) page that relies on social media and is run by young journalists.
The six-person team was forcibly disappeared, illegally detained, and interrogated under torture for several days before being charged with terrorism and spreading false news.
They remain in pretrial detention.
The crackdown then reached Mada Masr, one of Egypt’s most prominent independent outlets, and its founder and editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah.
On November 11, Attalah is due to stand trial for the second time in two weeks, this time on charges of spreading false news that carry a possible prison sentence.
The new trial follows her conviction on October 27, when a court found her guilty of managing a news website without a license in a single hearing marred by violations of her right to a fair trial.
She was given the maximum fine of EGP 3 million (about USD 55,000) and was forcibly removed from the courtroom and held until the fine was paid, seven hours later.
The court also ordered Mada Masr shut down and all of its equipment confiscated.
According to Mada Masr, the judge appointed a lawyer to represent Attalah even though eight of her own lawyers were in the courtroom and she objected.
The outlet says her objection was not recorded in the session’s minutes.
Amnesty International reports that Mada Masr applied for a license from the Supreme Council for Media Regulation in 2018 and 2020 and received no response, and submitted a new application in 2026.
Mada Masr was founded in 2013, an independent, critical, investigative outlet.
In other a decade of operation, Mada Masr was instrumental in informing the public about what is happening in Egypt, as well as in the region.
It gave a platform to torture victims and the families of political prisoners, and created space for debate on reproductive rights.
Its reporting on the genocides in Sudan and Gaza uncovered abuses and stood with refugees facing xenophobic attacks and security crackdowns.
The outlet has also long engaged with technology issues and advocated for a free, independent internet for the global majority.
The attack comes at a crucial point in Egypt’s and the region’s history, and goes beyond a question of human rights or activism.
At least 25 journalists are currently imprisoned in Egypt.

On Friday 30 October, Mada Masr published a statement on Instagram describing an “ongoing battle” and its efforts at “finding a legal way to continue [its] work while also taking care of each other in this moment of madness.
A wave of solidarity has mobilized supporters in Egypt and abroad.
“This is the kind of social movement, the doing of politics, how a newsroom is connected to its community, that we in our everyday practice would want to write about.
But this time it is us whom it was happening to,” the statement reads.
It concludes: “We are angry but hopeful, we are tired but insistent that our work must go on, that Lina should face neither prison nor fines, that all jailed journalists should be free.”

A joint statement led by Amnesty International and signed by organizations worldwide condemned “in the strongest terms the conviction of Lina Attalah, and the court’s order to shut down one of the country’s leading and last remaining independent newsrooms.
It called on Egyptian authorities to allow Mada Masr to operate freely.

items.title: In Kosovo, a new app makes reporting problems to the government fast and easy

s: It will cut the bureacratic red tape that plagues state institutions

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.
One of the biggest barriers for people’s effective engagement with the authorities in Kosovo is a confusing and unresponsive bureaucracy.

Whenever citizens want to report a problem in their community, such as potholes or illegal waste disposal, they are met with a system that requires them to know the roles and responsibilities of various state institutions and handle necessary paperwork themselves.

When submitted to the wrong agency or without proper documents, citizens’ complaints are either ignored or can take long periods to be processed, which discourages engagement and has an adverse effect on people’s trust in the government.
Ultimately, it deteriorates the already challenging situation regarding transparency, communication, and accountability of state bodies in Kosovo.

In 2026, a local non-governmental organization (NGO), Sbunker, responded to this challenge by creating an online platform called Kosovo.report to help citizens report their complaints to the authorities in a quick and easy manner.
Global Voices conducted an email interview with Hana Deva, project manager at SBunker, to learn more about their initiative.
The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Hana Deva (HD): Sbunker is a non-governmental organization founded in 2016, focused on providing analysis and informed perspectives on important political, economic, social, and cultural issues in Kosovo and the Western Balkans.
Through our Disinfo program, we monitor local and regional media content to identify and address disinformation.
Sbunker produces podcasts and other media content exploring political and social developments, philosophical, cultural, and theoretical discussions.
We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to create a direct form of civic engagement through technology.
This led to the development of Kosovo.report, a platform designed to give citizens a simple way to report problems and submit requests concerning their neighborhoods and local communities.
The platform is intended to act as a link between citizens and public institutions by helping these reports reach the relevant institutions and making the process more accessible to the citizens.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?
HD: Through our work in media and civic engagement, we became interested in how citizens communicate everyday problems in their communities to public institutions.

Research on public administration in Kosovo points to fragmented public service delivery, inconsistencies in administrative procedures and digital services, and continuing challenges in communication between citizens and institutions.
This can make the process of reporting an issue to the right department unclear.
Kosovo.report was developed with this challenge in mind.
The idea is to give citizens a more straightforward way to report an issue, without requiring them to first determine which institution or department is responsible.
Based on the type and location of the problem, the platform is designed to route the report to the appropriate department and allow the citizen to follow what happens afterwards.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?
HD: Our main work has been the development of Kosovo.report, from the initial concept to a functional platform now being prepared for its pilot phase.

Alongside this development, we have coordinated with the Municipality of Prishtina to determine how reports should reach the appropriate departments, and prepared a Memorandum of Understanding to formalise this cooperation.

items.title: Unpacking Hong Kong’s rule of law score according to the World Justice Project’s ranking

s: Hong Kong ranks 24th in rule of law index and is trending down

The Hong Kong anti-graft body, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), flaunted on X in early October that the city ranked in the top 10 globally and third in Asia in the “Absence of Corruption” category on the “ Rule of Law Index 2026 ” published by the World Justice Project (WJP).

However, the “Absence of Corruption” merely captures whether or not public officials from the administration, police force, and judiciary use their offices for private gain; this single factor does not mean a society is free from corruption, as institutional favoritism, such as political nepotism, legal discrimination, and cronyism, are equally dangerous abuses of power that create systematic injustice.

That’s why the WJP includes eight major factors in its index, and Hong Kong ranks 24th and scored 0.71 in the overall index among 143 countries, falling behind Australia (12), Singapore (14), Japan (15), and South Korea (20) in Asia and the Pacific.
Between 2016 and 2020, Hong Kong consistently ranked 16th overall in the index.

The eight factors considered in the Rule of Law Index are “constraints on government power,” “absence of corruption,” “open government,” “fundamental rights,” “order and security,” “regulatory enforcement,” “civil justice,” and “criminal justice.”

Hong Kong performs best in “order and security” (ranked seventh with a 0.92 score), “absence of corruption” (ranked 10th with a 0.83 score), and “regulatory enforcement (ranked 16th with a 0.79 score).
Among the subfactors of “order and security,” the city indeed has a relatively low crime rate (ranked eighth), and near-zero violent expression of grievance (ranked ninth).
In fact, the city has had hardly any protests since 2021, following the enactment of the National Security Law on June 30, 2020, and a heavy-handed crackdown on unauthorized protests.
However, civic conflict remains high (ranked 40th), as people resort to street fights to express their frustrations.

The average Hongkonger will likely disagree with the relatively high ranking of “regulatory enforcement,” particularly after the recent release of the Taipo Deadly Fire investigation report, which revealed that multiple Hong Kong government authorities, including the Housing Bureau, the Labor Department, the Fire Service Department, and the Buildings Department, had not effectively enforced related regulations, which could have prevented the death of 168 individuals on November 25, 2025.

Moreover, while Hongkongers have complained about tender rigging in building renovations for over a decade, it was only after the high-profile Taipo fire that the authorities vowed to actively investigate the construction sector.
Some fire victims also criticized the government’s buy-back plan as disrespectful of their private property rights.
Both effectiveness of regulatory enforcement and respecting property rights are subfactors of “regulatory enforcement” in the Index.
Hong Kong’s worst performance among the eight categories is “constraints in government’s power” (ranked 63rd with a 0.54 score) and “fundamental rights” (ranked 69th with a 0.55 score).
Hong Kong ranked 25th in “constraints in government’s power” in 2016, fell to 31st in 2020, then plummeted to 54th in 2022, and further tumbled to 63rd in 2025 and 2026.

The enactment of the National Security Law in Hong Kong on June 30, 2020, which empowered the Hong Kong government to shut down independent media outlets and NGOs, was the main driving force in the recent plunges.

Other factors included officials’ decision to rewrite electoral laws under the guiding principle of “patriots administering Hong Kong” in May 2021, the 2023 district council reform to restrict district councilors’ power and exclude oppositional figures, and the passage of domestic security law in March 2024 to outlaw acts including treason, espionage that harms the city, and incitement that provokes hatred.
Rights groups say all of these provisions have chilled civil society activity and encroached on citizens’ fundamental rights.

items.title: The Brazilian left’s quest to ‘tame’ Meta: A narrative of denouncement and resistance

s: Internet rights advocates and Lula da Silva campaigners challenge Meta’s alleged shadow banning
Over the years, Meta’s content moderation policies and governance practices have faced intense scrutiny and legal challenges over alleged political bias and a lack of transparency.

Since 2018, the Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh), a human rights organization advocating for Palestinian digital rights, has documented how Facebook’s (now Meta) moderation practices disproportionately affect Palestinian content.
In 2020, 7amleh launched a campaign challenging Facebook’s proposed hate speech policy, which considered “Zionist” a potential proxy for “Jew” or “Jewish.

More recently, in 2024, the organization collected 20 first-hand testimonies from Palestinian influencers, journalists, and media outlets documenting their experiences of Meta’s discriminatory content moderation practices.
In 2023, Human Rights Watch also reported “systemic online censorship” against voices in support of Palestine and Palestinian human rights,

In 2022, Tom Vandendriessche, a Belgian politician and Member of the European Parliament (MEP) representing the far-right Vlaams Belang (Flemish Interest) party, partially prevailed in a legal case against Meta concerning a shadow ban imposed on his account in 2021 after the company removed several posts alleging a breach of its Terms of Service (ToS) and Facebook Community Guidelines (FCG).

A Belgian court ordered the company to compensate the politician for financial and reputational damages, finding that its actions had significantly restricted his ability to engage in political discourse online and that Meta had failed to provide adequate transparency or effective avenues for redress.

In 2026, Meta has faced significant criticism in Brazil and internationally from internet rights watchdogs over political bias, algorithmic interference, and the selective suppression of content perceived as favoring far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro during the October 2026 Brazilian presidential election.

Using the slogan Meta não se meta (roughly, “Meta, stay out of it”), which plays on the Portuguese word meta, derived from the verb meter (“to get involved” or “to interfere”), internet rights defenders and current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s followers and allies sought not only to expose alleged Meta’s shadow-banning practices during Brazil’s 2026 presidential election but also to mobilize Brazilians to demand a fairer digital space collectively.

In October 2026, during the Brazilian presidential runoff election campaign, a coalition of Brazilian civil society organizations, social movements, and digital rights advocacy groups, including CTRL+Z, Código Não Binário, ARTIGO 19 (Article 19 Brasil), Sleeping Giants Brasil, and others, launched the webpage naosemeta.com.br as part of their initiative to denounce electoral interference and algorithmic bias.

The site offered three ways for people to hold Meta accountable online: email Meta; message Meta’s General Director in Brazil on LinkedIn; and comment on Meta Ceo Mark Zuckerberg’s latest Instagram post.

It also shared a space for those wishing to join and sign a petition to the Superior Electoral Court and an extrajudicial notification, a formal written communication sent on October 19 to put Meta on notice and demand that it recognize the technical flaws in its advertising, moderation, and artificial intelligence (AI) systems, and the distribution and availability of user-generated content and campaign materials in Brazil — which these organizations claim disadvantaged, in particular, candidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The online strategy to hold Meta accountable was accompanied by a protest in front of Meta’s offices on October 19, where participants called for respect for Brazil’s digital sovereignty, with the Homeless Workers Movement’s Technology Center among the loudest voices.
For those reclaiming digital sovereignty, the company’s actions stem from the relationship between U.S.

President Donald Trump and Brazil’s ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, father of Flávio Bolsonaro, and the influence the current U.S. administration has over big-tech owners — they consider Meta to be facilitating foreign interference.

items.title: Caloundra wins first game in Australian soccer's Football Queensland Premier League 2 competition

s: Caloundra got their first season in the Football Queensland Premier League 2 (FQPL 2) competition underway with a 4 goals to 2 win over Brisbane Knights FC at their home ground in Meridan Plains, Australia on Saturday night.
"Starting the game that quickly, it just makes life a lot easier," Caloundra player Ethan Galbraith said.
"It was surprising but amazing at the same time.
I think we started fast like we wanted to.
And we got on top.
And once you do that to a team, obviously it makes it hard for them to get back into it.
But credit to them.
Second half with the man down, they really battled and made it difficult for us.
It's obviously a tough place to come.
Travel up the Coast on a weekend."
It was a tough away trip for the Brisbane Knights.
Their first twenty minutes were slow with a bit of ill-discipline, according to their coach, Rob Shaw.
"[It] cost us, I think, in that first half," Shaw said.
"[We] changed shape in the second half, showed, the boys settled, started to play football, a little bit better football.
It actually worked in some ways, even the man down.
The boys worked hard.
It was a bit of a mountain to climb, though, after the first half, but can't fault the effort though from the boys."
Caloundra will now travel to play Moreton City Excelsior while Brisbane Knights host the Samford Rangers.
"I think they're a pretty tough team," Galbraith said.
"We'll be up against it next week but looking forward to the challenge.
They've got a lot of good players in there. [They're a] very good team.
So we'll be up against it but ready for it."

items.title: Randwick City Council opens public consultation about parking near beaches: ''To pay or not to pay?''

s: On Wednesday, Randwick City Council, a municipality on the east coast of Sydney, New South Wales, Australia, opened a public consultation period focused on introducing parking fees at beaches within the Randwick area.
The consultation, affecting up to thousands of beachgoers in peak hours on hot summer weekends, is set to close on April 15.

The council mailed the consultation paper version to all residents and added to Randwick's "Have Your Say" portal with an online form and a note that feedback may also be provided by phone and in person.

The Council noted the beaches received a lot of non-local traffic, allegedly reaching 84% at certain beaches, according to mobile phone data collected by Veitch Lister Consulting (VLC), a United Kingdom and Australian firm.
The revenue from paid parking would help towards beaches cleaning, maintenance, and improving the quality of amenities, the Council wrote on the public consultation page.
The Council estimated implementing the proposal would require A$3.6 million expenditure and would generate yearly A$6 million revenue.
Randwick includes the Clovelly, Coogee, Maroubra, Malabar, Little Bay (Malabar Beach), La Perouse (Frenchmans Bay) and Yarra Bay areas.
The proposal stated that new signage and parking meters would be installed in late 2026 and 2027 if the proposal was approved.
A Wikinews contributor visited the area, noting previously the parking was time-limited but predominantly free, with selected sections designated as paid parking.
Parking at Arden St. was free, while parking at Coogee Oval or near Coogee Pavilion required a fee from 2003 to 2016.
Meanwhile, parking near Manly and Bondi beaches outside the Randwick area required a fee in many spots and streets immediately adjacent to the beach as of 2026.
Near Manly, a multi-level paid car park was available in a nearby shopping center.

items.title: US President Donald Trump appears to wear makeup after apparent rash breaks out on neck, reports say

s: On Tuesday, a rash that reporters had observed on US President Donald Trump's neck in photos from a Medal of Honor ceremony at the White House one day earlier appeared to have been covered up.
One media source indicated the substance used was cosmetic makeup, although Trump's physician, Dr. Sean Barbabella, told the source the rash had been covered up by a "very common cream."
President Trump has worn makeup in public before.
He once wore makeup to obscure bruises on his hands, which White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, stated were inflicted from "shaking hands all day every day.
Trump himself has attributed the bruises to his use of aspirin, of which he says he takes excessive amounts.
Trump said, "They say aspirin is good for thinning out the blood, and I don’t want thick blood pouring through my heart.
I want nice, thin blood pouring through my heart.
Does that make sense?"

items.title: Monta publishes its 2025 EV charger ranking, including hardware performance

s: The Danish firm Monta published a performance ranking of electric vehicle (EV) chargers on Wednesday.
The firm analysed 260,000 EV chargers connected to its platform, which were located in Europe.
In the publication, the firm showed the chargers ranked by their "performance score".
The firm calculated this score metric from two parameters — the charger uptime, and the percent of charge sessions that went successful without hardware or software or user interruptions.
The AC — slower chargers — and DC — fast chargers — ranking was provided in two separate tables.
AC chargers performance was topped by a Mennekes EV charger, with performance score 94.65.
Among DC chargers, five charger models by Alpitronic took the top spots, with performance score reaching 96.54.

The Driven, an Australian news site, noted that '9 out of 10' of the top performing DC chargers from Monta's report were available for sale, and were in use — by Ampol AmpCharge and BP Pulse — in Australia.
The firm noted the published results provided motivation for EV chargers to adopt these benchmarks in marketing, and further develop their products to increase performance and uptime.

A volunteer Wikinews reporter reached out to Monta, and Monta has clarified that they also have some EV chargers on their platform in Asia, Oceania, and North America, however excluded them from the ranking due to small quantities.
Monta also noted they were planning to release quarterly EV charger updates in 2026, and yearly EV charger ranking reports with awards.
The Monta's EV charger ranking program was launched in June last year.
Monta won the best EV app/software at the E-Mobility Awards 2023.

items.title: Moreton Bay illegally evicted homeless campers, Queensland Supreme Court rules

s: This past Friday, Justice Paul Smith of the Supreme Court of Queensland ruled that the City of Moreton Bay Council, immediately north of Brisbane, Australia, acted unlawfully when it removed several homeless people camping in public parks last year.

The court concluded the Council breached the law by providing insufficient time for the homeless people to find alternative accommodation and by disposing of their personal belongings without consent.

In the judgement, Justice Smith said the Council made "errors of law" finding that the Council's seizure and disposal of the property of eight homeless people at Eddie Hyland Park — including their tents and other personal belongings — without consent in April and May last year violated human rights.
Although the eviction involved eight campers at the park, the legal case was brought by eleven applicants who said they were affected by the Council's enforcement actions.
The judgement noted that the Council would still be allowed to remove campers from public parks provided this was done "lawfully".
On Friday, the Council published a statement noting that eight homeless people had taken the Council to court and linking to the Supreme Court judgement.
In that statement Council stated it would continue enforcing its ban on camping on public land.
Responsibility for providing shelter to homeless people rested with the Queensland state government according to the Council.
The court scheduled the next hearing in three weeks to determine relief and costs.
Basic Rights Queensland and the Queensland Human Rights Commission supported the campers in the legal proceedings.
The Council's actions followed its decision earlier in February last year to ban camping on public land, which made camping illegal on public land within the Council from March 12, 2025.

items.title: Australia grants refuge to five Iranian women's national soccer team players

s: Early Tuesday morning, Australia government officials issued humanitarian visas to five members of Iran's national women's football team.

The players refused to sing the Iranian anthem while at the Women's Asian Cup last week. if the visas had not been granted, the five players potentially faced serious punishment on their return to Iran, as Iranian media has labeled them "traitors".
Tony Burke, Minister for Home Affairs of Australia, sent a message on X on Tuesday stating that the five players were "welcome to stay in Australia, to be safe and have a home here".
The players are Zahra Ghanbari (captain), Fatemeh Pasandideh, Zahra Sarbali, Atefeh Ramezanizadeh, and Mona Hamoudi.
Tuesday afternoon, however, the rest of the Iranian national women's soccer team travelled to Gold Coast airport by bus.
As of Tuesday morning, authorities said these remaining Iranian women's soccer team members had not requested asylum, though were welcomed to do so.
Protesters surrounded the bus and some were lying on the ground to stop the bus, and had to be moved by police.

Due to reported threats from Iranian media and officials, in Australia, local police worked with the authorities and provided a safe place for the players to stay, as well as increased presence when the players were traveling.

items.title: Former Major League Baseball pitcher Julio Teherán retires

s: Julio Teherán, a two-time Major League Baseball All-Star, announced his retirement from baseball on Monday, at the age of 35.
The decision came two days after he was scratched from a scheduled start for Team Colombia in the 2026 World Baseball Classic (WBC) due to a shoulder injury.
Teherán had helped Team Colombia secure a 3-1 victory over Team Panama in the WBC before announcing his retirement.
Teherán had a thirteen-year MLB career, during which he primarily played for the Atlanta Braves, but also played for the Los Angeles Angels, Detroit Tigers, Milwaukee Brewers, and New York Mets.
He made his MLB debut with the Braves in 2011 at the age of 20 and spent his first nine seasons with the team, earning All-Star selections in 2014 and 2016.
Over his MLB career, Teherán compiled a 81-82 record, with a 3.85 ERA, 1.223 WHIP, and 1,260 strikeouts in 1,470.2 innings.
He had spent the 2022 and 2025 seasons playing in the Mexican Baseball League.

items.title: PM of Australia sends E-7A Wedgetail and air-to-air missiles to UAE

s: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said that, in response to United Arab Emirates call for help, Australia would deploy E-7A Wedgetail, a long-range reconnaissance plane, to help Gulf Arab states defend against attacks from Iran.
The Australian Defence Force said the plane is able to survey four million square kilometers with a powerful radar.
Government officials said the plane would be manned by around 85 Australian defence force (ADF) personnel.
Additionally, Australia would supply middle range air to air missiles, at the request of United Arab Emirates, that could down enemy's drones.
Foreign affairs correspondent at ABC News, Stephen Dziedzic, published a piece on Wednesday noting that from a legal perspective, Australia is at war.
He stated that not being an attacker, and not entering Iran, did not preclude Australia from joining a war.

The correspondent referenced article 51 from United Nations charter about "collective self-defence", which could involve, for example, providing support or intelligence to one of the participants of a war.
The correspondent raised concern that move could make Australia a potential target for attacks from, for example, Iran.

items.title: NSW government proposes rezoning to create residences midway between Sydney and Parramatta

s: The government of New South Wales (NSW), Australia announced plans to rezone the 113-hectare Burwood North precinct this Tuesday.
The plan included building 18,300 new homes in the area, and building a new metro station.
This would position the area as a residential hub between Sydney CBD and Parramatta, shortening commute times down to ten minutes, the proposal said.

With allowance for up to 42 storey residential buildings, the government proposal involved a requirement that at least 5% of the new homes were "affordable housing", offered at a lower rental price to lower income households.
Burwood North Station, scheduled to open in 2032, would provide easier access to retail outlets and businesses located near Parramatta Road, and reduce load on existing train and bus networks.
The proposal text noted it would create 3,900 new jobs to implement the changes.
The proposal was a part of Parramatta Road Corridor Urban Transformation Strategy.
The NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure was listed as a contact for inquiries and feedback.

items.title: US president Donald Trump demands the unconditional surrender of Iran

s: Last Friday, United States President Donald Trump demanded the "unconditional surrender" of Iran via his Truth Social platform.
The declaration came as the war in Iran had gone on for a week.
Trump has also demanded more "acceptable" leadership in the country.
Trump wrote that once "acceptable" leadership was selected in Iran, the US and its allies would make Iran "economically bigger, better, and stronger than ever before."
On Saturday, in an address to the nation, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said that Trump's demand is a "dream they should send to their grave."
A week ago, the United States and Israel attacked Iran, and killed various government officials, including the supreme leader of Iran, Ali Khamenei, in strikes.
In retaliation for the attacks, Iran has bombed Middle Eastern countries including Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Oman, according to SBS News.
In the Saturday address, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian apologized for attacks on regional countries, Jakarta Globe reported.
The Globe also reported that 1,230 people were killed in Iran and that six US troops were killed.
Leavitt has stated that the war would likely last four to six weeks.

items.title: Australian Minister for Energy lowers fuel standards for 60 days amid rising oil prices, panic buying

s: Chris Bowen, Australian Minister for Climate Change and Energy, allowed the usage of dirtier fuel with elevated sulfur content for 60 days, he announced on Thursday.
As a part of the change, the oil refineries were required to prioritise supply to farmers in rural areas.
This decision followed issues with oil exports caused by the ongoing Middle East conflict, as fuel prices rose rapidly to over A$2/L.
The lower quality oil was previously exported to countries with lower fuel standards.
With the new temporarily changes in place, it would now be allowed to be used in Australia.
One of the two oil refineries, Ampol, noted rural areas supply would be prioritised.
Additionally, Bowen announced Australia would release 100 million liters from its reserve oil supply per month, in response to a request from the International Energy Agency (IEA).
The issue appeared related to the growing demand while supply was essentially unchanged.
As people stockpiled fuel, and the demand has doubled, there were concerns over panic buying by Australians.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese commented on longer term impacts of the situation on economics in Australia, talking with ABC Television on Thursday.

President of the National Farmer Federation commented noting the government regulation was direly needed in this situation as farmers and fishers were struggling to access fuel, especially in remote areas.

He also noted that government should prepare strategies in case the situation 'deteriorates', mentioning access to diesel was a pre-requisite for the farmers running the agricultural areas, collecting crops, transporting crops, and providing food to the country.
In reserve, Australia had 36 days worth of petrol, 32 days worth of diesel, and 29 days worth of jet fuel, respectively.
These fell short of the 90 days requirement under obligations for the IEA, of which Australia is a member.
Opposition was calling on the government to ensure fuel security, ABC News reported.

items.title: Caloundra win round 3 game in Australian soccer's Football Queensland Premier League 2 competition

s: Caloundra have won their round 3 Football Queensland Premier League 2 game against Pine Hills 5 goals to 2 at Meridan Plains, Queensland, Australia on Sunday.
"Two [wins] from three [games]" said Caloundra captain Kaine Frew.
"I think we'll probably be in the top four now.
Not a bad start.
It's still very early days.
Yeah, you can't get too ahead of yourselves.
I think you've just got to take it week by week for the moment."
Riley Campbell opened the scoring for Caloundra in the second minute.
Aaron Doherty levelled the score two minutes later.
Alex Witte took Pine Hills ahead in the eleventh minute.
Darryl Barton brought the scores level again in the thirteenth minute.
Barton scored his second goal to retake the lead do Caloundra in the twenty seventh minute.
Caloundra lead three goals to two at the break.
Jake Debbage added Caloundra's fourth in the fifty first minute before Mackenar Bradfield took the score line to five goals to three in the ninetieth minute.
"It was a pretty even game, first half," said Pine Hills assistant coach Daniel Cunha.
"[We] conceded three goals.
Lazy goals, in our opinion.
But we managed to bounce back with two goals.
Managed to stay in the game, but yeah, second half with early, conceded early goals, so that was it for us."
Caloundra host Mitchellton on Saturday, while Pine Hills travel to Samford.

items.title: "One Battle After Another" wins 6 Oscars including Best Picture

s: One Battle After Another was the big winner at the 98th Academy Awards ceremony, held on Sunday, March 15 at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles, California.
The film received six Oscars including Best Picture.
Director Paul Thomas Anderson personally won Best Director and Best Adapted Screenplay, in addition to being one of the producers who received the Best Picture award.

The other three Oscars which One Battle After Another received were for Best Editing and Best Casting, the first time the latter award has been presented, and for Sean Penn as Best Supporting Actor, the third Oscar of his career.
Sinners, which had set a record by earning sixteen Oscar nominations, won awards in four categories: Best Actor for Michael B.
Jordan, Best Original Screenplay for Ryan Coogler, Best Original Score for Ludwig Goransson, and Best Cinematography for Autumn Durald Arkapaw.
Arkapaw is the first woman to win an Academy Award for Best Cinematography.
Two other films won multiple Oscars.
Frankenstein won Best Production Design, Best Costume Design, and Best Makeup and Hairstyling.
KPop Demon Hunters won Best Animated Feature and Best Song for Golden.
Best Supporting Actress: Amy Madigan for Weapons
Best International Feature: Sentimental Value, from Norway (directed by Joachim Trier)
Best Visual Effects: Avatar: Fire and Ash
Best Documentary Feature: Mr. Nobody Against Putin
Best Documentary Short: All the Empty Rooms
Best Animated Short: The Girl Who Cried Pearls
Best Live Action Short: The Singers and Two People Exchanging Saliva (tie)
The Oscar ceremony was hosted by Conan O'Brien.

items.title: South Korean military halts small firearms drills after stray bullet strikes young girl on playground

s: On Tuesday, officials for the South Korean Army said at a press conference that they were suspending all scheduled drills involving smaller firearms such as rifles and handguns.

The decision was made in response to an incident earlier in the week on Monday that resulted in a young girl at a children playground in Daegu being injured near the neck by an alleged stray bullet from a military drill at nearby military facility.
Her injuries were not life-threatening and she was released from the hospital.
Her name was not released to the general public.
Investigations into the circumstances leading up the incident were said to be underway.
The incident raised questions regarding the military's practice of conducting shooting drills in close proximity to civilian territory.
A spokesperson for the army confirmed that a firearms drill had indeed been taking place at the same time the girl reported being struck.
The incident came a year after the South Korean Army accidentally bombed a small village near the North Korean border, injuring 30 civilians, while conducting a drill with US forces.

items.title: Musique Libre Femmes plays for Women's History Month at Tompkins Square Library in New York City

s: On Thursday, March 12, 2026, the Tompkins Square Library in New York City hosted a concert by Musique Libre Femmes, in its basement performance space.
This performance featured Cheryl Pyle on flute, Ayumi Ishito on saxophones, and Roberta Piket on piano.
There were approximately fifteen people in attendance.
Wikinews attended the event and took several photos and recordings to transcribe for this news report.
The performance started at 6:00 p.m.
New York Time (2200 UTC), and was introduced by director of adult services Jeffrey Katz.
After explaining that the series was ongoing, and announcing upcoming performance dates as well, he introduced the performers:
((Jeffrey Katz)) So we are celebrating Women's History Month with Musique Libre Femmes.
And this is a group of all women free jazz improvisers who compose, create spontaneous, in-the-moment music.
The group consists of some of the most experienced improvisers of the New York Jazz scene.
And they have recently played at the Lady Got Chops Festival, the Downtown Music Gallery, and many of the New York City Jazz venues.
After which, the performance began and lasted about forty minutes, after which the audience applauded.
After the event, Pyle had the following comments about the series:

((Cheryl Pyle)) I started the group Musique Libre Femmes, Free Music Women, because I saw a film called Fire Music, and they interviewed Carla Bley and Ingrid Sertso, and they didn't talk about any of their music.
And they didn't talk about any other women improvisers, Barbara Donald, you know, anybody.
So I wanted to do some concerts with all women.
((CP)) And today we played with Roberta Piket on piano and Ayumi Ishito on tenor sax and soprano sax and myself, Cheryl Pyle on C-flute, piccolo and alto flute.
And we're here at the Tompkins Square Library in the East Village and we just had a wonderful concert.

items.title: United States announces blockade on the Strait of Hormuz

s: On Sunday, United States President Donald Trump announced on Truth Social that the US is imposing a blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.
According to Trump, the blockade was in effect as of 10:00 a.m.
Eastern Time (1400 UTC).
The blockade was imposed following the collapse of talks held in Islamabad between the United States and Iran.
"Effective immediately, the United States Navy, the finest in the world, will be BLOCKADING any and all ships trying to enter, or leave, the Strait of Hormuz," Trump declared.
According to The Guardian, oil prices briefly rose above US$100 a barrel following news of the blockade, before easing back to just over US$99; gas prices also increased.
Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf posted on X to "Enjoy the current pump figures.
With the so-called 'blockade', soon you'll be nostalgic for $4–$5 gas.
He further stated that Iran would respond in kind to both escalation and diplomacy, warning that it would "fight" if confronted militarily but would "deal with logic" if approached constructively.

China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed hope that the ceasefire would remain stable, stating that Beijing is willing to cooperate with all parties to "guarantee the uninterrupted flow of energy supplies," and that stability in the Strait of Hormuz is critically important to China.

items.title: Pope Leo XIV visits four nations in Africa

s: Pope Leo XIV arrived by plane in Algeria on Monday, April 13, beginning his apostolic visit to Africa.

A senior Vatican official told the BBC the pope wanted to "turn the world's attention to Africa"; the BBC reported the eleven-day visit would address themes of peace, migration, and interfaith dialogue.
The trip also includes stops in Cameroon, Angola, and Equatorial Guinea.
The visit marked Leo's second major foreign trip as pope since his election in May last year.
The regions of the continent being visited are among the quickest growing in Catholicism in the world.
There were an estimated 288 million Catholics in Africa in 2024, making up more than one-fifth of the world's total.
His first stop in Algeria marked the first papal visit to the country in history.
While there, Leo planned to visit several locations including ancient Christian sites in Annaba and the Great Mosque of Algiers in the capital before departing.

The stop was followed by a visit to Cameroon, where Leo addressed about 120,000 people in Douala, encouraging young people to turn away from violence and corruption and advocating for justice and peace.
He was expected to make a planned visit to a Catholic hospital in the city before traveling to Yaoundé to meet with students from the Catholic University of Central Africa.
On Sunday, April 19, the pope arrived in Angola, where he met with President João Lourenço and other officials.
He later addressed a crowd gathered near the capital, Luanda.
He was also expected to visit the town of Muxima, the country's main Christian pilgrimage site.

After Angola, the pope arrived on Tuesday, April 21, in Equatorial Guinea, where, according to the BBC, Catholics make up more than 70% of the central African nation, for the final leg of the visit, before his scheduled return to the Vatican.

items.title: Wikimedia Foundation closes Wikinews after 21 years

s: The Board of Trustees of the Wikimedia Foundation announced on March 30 its decision to close all language editions of the project.

In the announcement, a representative from Wikimedia Foundation cited motivations such as "long-term sustainability, levels of community activity, and the availability of reliable news coverage on other platforms".
The announcement stated that all Wikinews editions—referring to the multiple language sections of Wikinews—would "transition to read-only mode" on May 4.
The announcement did not mention the time zone when the wiki would go in read-only mode; but Wikinews operated under the UTC timezone.

In the announcement message, WMF trustee Victoria Doronina said, "We thank all contributors who have participated in Wikinews over the years and helped build a unique experiment in collaborative journalism within the Wikimedia movement.
We understand that some of them may be disappointed by this decision.
To our regret, the project wasn't able to fulfil its promise, and many of its functions were eclipsed by the notable news coverage in Wikipedias."
According to the WMF, most traffic to Wikinews came in the form of web crawlers and bots, as opposed to humans.
Per the Wikimedia Cloud statistics in the past one year, both, English and Chinese Wikinews received more traffic from humans as compared to crawlers.
The foundation stated in its closure recommendation that it is "difficult to claim that it is disseminating educational content and, even more so, that it is doing so effectively and globally."
On March 31, users from different countries and regions started discussions regarding moving the Wikinews content and community to another website at Wikimedia's Meta-Wiki.

Miraheze and Wikimedia NYC were in discussion of continuing the hosting as Wikinews Pulse, with a restructure to increase multilingual support and try new outputs, according to a note by a Wikimedia volunteer User:Pharos.
However, at the time of publishing this report, they had not provided an estimated time the project would be restarted.
Wikinews was a sister project of other Wikimedia initiatives.
Some of the other sister projects includes Wikipedia, Wiktionary, and Wikimedia Commons.
All of these Wikimedia projects support the dissemination of free knowledge and media.
The future of Wikinews was raised for consideration in June, with a WMF task force recommending the project's closure, followed by a period of public consultation about Wikinews.
After this process, the Board announced in March that the 31 active editions of Wikinews would be placed in read-only mode indefinitely.
Wikinews was launched in November 2004.
It was first proposed by an anonymous contributor in January 2003 and faced a community vote that ended 151 yea and 59 nay, leading to the first demo going live in October 2004.
The English-language Wikinews was formally created December 2 of that year, with German following one day later.
The project's early development followed a series of community discussions and milestones in late 2004 and early 2005.
A non-binding straw poll on content licensing began on October 26, 2004, alongside discussions on the project's scope and policies.
The initial demo site, hosted at demo.wikinews.org, was later moved to the English Wikinews domain on December 2 of that year.

Following the launch of the English and German editions in December 2004, additional language editions were created in early 2005, including Dutch, French, Swedish, Spanish, Bulgarian, Polish, Romanian, and Portuguese.
The project also adopted a logo in February 2005 through a community voting process.
While many Wikinews articles were synthesized from other news sources, the project also posted original reporting.
The purpose of this activity was to add exclusive content which would not be available elsewhere on the web or on television.
These original reports included interviews with people such as Shimon Peres, then-president of Israel; U.S.
Senator Sam Brownback; journalist Gay Talese; and voice actor Billy West.
A 2005 article featuring original reporting, Unrest in Belize, was cited by Wikipedia co-founder Jimmy Wales as Wikinews's first scoop.

items.title: Opposition leader Tarique Rahman returns to Bangladesh after 17 years

s: Tarique Rahman, the acting chairman of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) returned to Bangladesh on December 25, 2025, landing in Dhaka after 17 years in self-imposed exile in London.
His arrival marks a significant development in the country's political landscape following the ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024.
Rahman is the son of Khaleda Zia, the official chairperson of the party and former Prime Minister of Bangladesh.
Upon landing at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka, Rahman was greeted by thousands of Bangladesh Nationalist Party supporters amid tight security.

Accompanied by his wife, Zubaida Rahman, and daughter, Zaima Rahman, he addressed a rally, emphasizing national unity, inclusivity across religious lines, and the vision of a democratic and economically strong Bangladesh.
He drew parallels to the country's 1971 war of independence.
Rahman, aged 60, left Bangladesh in 2008 for medical treatment after being released on bail following 18 months in detention during the military-backed government's rule from 2006 to 2008.
He was convicted in absentia of charges including corruption, money laundering, and involvement in a 2004 grenade attack on a political rally for his political rival, Sheikh Hasina.
These convictions were overturned or stayed after Hasina's government's fall.
His return comes amid preparations for general elections scheduled for early 2026, under an interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus.
The elections follow a student-led uprising in 2024 that resulted in Hasina's removal and her subsequent flight to India.
The protests, initially sparked by opposition to a job quota system, escalated into broader anti-government demonstrations, leading to an estimated 1,400 deaths according to United Nations figures.
Hasina has since been sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity related to the crackdown.
According to a December poll by the International Republican Institute, the BNP is the frontrunner for the election with 30 percent support.
The party has recently distanced itself from allies like Jamaat-e-Islami to adopt a more centrist approach.
However, challenges remain, including integrating party factions, maintaining law and order, and addressing potential unrest from Awami League supporters.
The Awami League was not allowed to participate in the elections.
Rahman's mother, Khaleda Zia, 80, is hospitalised in critical condition since November 2025.
She was the BNP's acting chairman since 2018 and was jailed most of the times during Hasina's administration.

items.title: United States capture Venezuelan president, Nicolás Maduro

s: The president of Venezuela, Nicolás Maduro, has been captured by the United States on Saturday at around 3 am UTC-4, according to a post by US president Donald Trump on social media.
Trump has told reporters Maduro had been “in a house that was more like a fortress”, in the country’s capital, Caracas.
Trump justified this action by claiming that Maduro is the leader of the Cartel de los Soles, and pushing illegal immigration of dangerous individuals in the United States.
Yván Gil Pinto, Venezuela’s foreign minister, said the country has requested a United Nations Security Council meeting to be held after the attack.
The BBC reports airstrikes in Caracas targeting La Carlota, an airbase and Fort Tiuna, a military base where the United States suspected Maduro to be located, and in other locations.
According to local authorities there has been civilian deaths and injuries, but the exact numbers are still unknown.
It was also reported by the BBC that the operation was orchestrated by a {CIA infiltration of the Venezuelan government.
France 24 reported that the CIA had been monitoring his “every movement since August”, despite Maduro’s efforts to change location regularly.
It was also reported that the operation involved more than 150 military aircraft, including one helicopter that was to capture Maduro.

According to the United States authorities, the Delta Force special operation force, arrived at Maduro’s location at “2:01 a.m. local time” and were able to capture him before he could get into his solid steel safe room (sources contradict however, on his exact location at that point.
Some sources reported that Trump said Maduro was almost in his safe room whilst others said he was sleeping in his bed).
They then relocated the “indicted persons” on a ship after crossing the coastline of Venezuela at 3:29 am.

Trump later revealed that Maduro’s wife, Cilia Flores, was also captured, and both were on board the USS Iwo Jima (LHD-7) with destination the southern district of New York, ultimately to be prosecuted.

Attorney General Pam Bondi was quoted by the BBC saying “[he will] face the full wrath of American justice on American soil in American courts” and, according to CNN, announced an indictment for leading “state‐sponsored gangs” and supporting drug trafficking.
Venezuelan authorities also reported other strikes, said to be made with the intent of seizing their oil and minerals, and have declared national emergency.
They, along with Cuba, Colombia, Iran and Russia, have denounced the action as a “serious military aggression”.
Argentine’s president, Javier Milei supported the action.
